In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This is an exciting paper demonstrating roles for cortical astrocytes in sleep. Activity in networks of neurons throughout the brain is different when an animal is asleep compared to when it is awake, and it has long been speculated that astrocytes, non-neuronal cells in the brain, may be partly responsible for regulating neuronal network activity during sleep. However, solid evidence has been largely lacking until recently. This paper plays an important in elucidating the connection between astrocytes and sleep, and suggests that astrocytes play a homeostatic role in regulating neurons during sleep.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cortical astrocytes independently regulate sleep depth and duration via separate GPCR pathways" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Laura Colgin as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary

This work builds on several recent publications implicating astrocyte control of sleep but represents an several new findings that provide new insight toward elucidating the mechanisms underlying the reported observations. The paper presents high quality data, rigorous experiments and analyses. Overall the paper is well written; however, there are several (relatively straightforward) points to address prior to publication as summarized below from both reviewers.

Revisions for this paper:

– Please revise to increase clarity in text and figures as suggested.

– The temporal relationships between astrocyte signals and SWA changes is complex, with SWA decreasing before astrocyte calcium events and increasing after. This is interpreted as astrocytes having a homeostatic effect on SWA. Causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret, in part because the homeostatic effect may involve more than just astrocytes but also neurons or other cell types. Including imaging data of cortical astrocytes together with nearby cortical neurons could help clarify the temporal relationship between these cells. If this data is not available, please address this possibility.

– Along similar lines, the authors demonstrate sufficiency, but do not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways because of the difficulty in knocking them out. Please temper claims and address alternative interpretations in the Discussion.

– Is CNO is equally efficacious at Gi and Gq DREADDs for downstream signaling in astrocytes? Please comment or determine if the Gi and Gq DREADDs are expressed to the same level in astrocytes (see points 3,4 reviewer #1 and related comments by reviewer 2).

– In this study SWA, measured through LFP, is used as the primary measure of sleep; however SWA can also be measured from EEG, a more common way to define sleep states. Can data be included that quantifies the degree to which these are correlated? Other indicators of sleep include arousal threshold could also help show relationships between their LFP-measure of SWA and such other measures? Please include or address potential caveats in paper if data cannot be included.

Reviewer #1:

The paper by Poskanzer and colleagues presents a detailed description of astrocyte calcium dynamics during natural sleep and then explores the consequences on slow wave activity (SWA) of stimulating astrocyte Gi and Gq DREADDs. Overall, this study builds on several years' worth of work by many labs showing or at least suggesting potentially important roles of astrocytes in sleep. As such, the topic and the data are not completely novel, but to their credit the authors have performed in depth analyses that go far deeper than previous studies. The depth of the analyses and the rigor of the approach outweigh any concerns that may linger regarding past work and push this study into a category of paper that is much needed and valued in the field. Seems highly appropriate for eLife.

No major concerns.

Reviewer #2:

This is an exciting paper showing relationships between sleep and Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling pathways in astrocytes. The paper demonstrates correlations between astrocyte calcium signals and sleep signatures such as slow-wave activity (SWA) measured with LFP in cortex. Astrocytes show activity changes near SWA changes such as at sleep-wake transitions. These are investigated using Gi- and Gq-DREADDs and it is found that astrocytes have a causal effect on SWA and the frequency of sleep-wake transitions. These results provide evidence for a role for astrocytes in controlling sleep-related SWA, with separate effects on sleep depth and duration depending on which GPCR pathway is perturbed.

This work is related to other recent publications implicating astrocyte control of sleep and contains a multitude of new findings. These are very interesting and elucidating while also pointing toward directions of research needed for determining the molecular and mechanisms underlying the reported observations.

1) The conclusions are somewhat indirect when it comes to causal relationships and mechanisms. The temporal relationships between astrocyte signals and SWA changes is complex, with SWA decreasing before astrocyte calcium events and increasing after. This is interpreted as astrocytes having a homeostatic effect on SWA. Causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret, in part because the homeostatic effect may involve more than just astrocytes but also neurons, including neurons whose activity is less visible in LFP measurements of SWA. Although this may be outside the scope of this study, if the authors have imaging data available of cortical astrocytes together with nearby cortical neurons (that is, a more direct measure of nearby neuron activity than LFP), this might clarify the temporal relationship between these cells.

2) The paper demonstrates sufficiency, astrocytes can change cortical SWA and sleep duration, but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior because of the difficulty in knocking them out. Can the text (perhaps the title) be adjusted to reflect this?

3) The authors show that there is inverse relationship between SWA amplitude and astrocytic calcium events in Figure 1H, with higher calcium activities associated with lower SWA. Gi-DREADD activation by CNO can increase astrocytic calcium events, and also increase SWA. Can the authors discuss this changed relationship in more depth? In addition, Gq-DREADD can change sleep time and sleep-wake transition, but not change SWA. Do these results indicate that astrocytic calcium may be not directly affect sleep duration or depth, but some other signal downstream of the GPCR?

4) In the Gi-DREADD experiments, the IP3R2-/- mouse is tested and found to lead to a smaller effect of CNO on SWA. Why was the IP3R2-/- not included in the Gq-DREADD experiments? Was that based on the assumption that there would be no difference, since Ca events disappeared in the Gq experiments?

5) It is unclear what the true effect of the Gq-DREADDs is on astrocyte calcium because activity is only represented by event rate (extracted by AQuA) and not as Ca concentration. Does event rate go down because Ca concentration drops to low levels and shows no dynamics, or because Ca concentration saturates and shows no dynamics due to a ceiling effect (as in the wake cocktail experiments)? This could be measured as absolute fluorescence of GCaMP. Interpretation of the results could change depending on which one of these is true. For example, saturated calcium could indicate an “unphysiological” state of astrocytes that can have consequences on the network that may not occur during natural sleep/wake.

6) The conclusion that "Gq-induced Ca2+ is necessary for sleep-wake transitions" (text and Figure 6) seems somewhat overstated. The Gq-DREADDs are a useful way to perturb calcium dynamics and this leads to changes in sleep-wake transitions, but it was not shown that without Gq sleep-wake transitions disappear. Also the effect demonstrated (Figure 6F for example) is partial. It seems appropriate to rephrase this statement.

7) SWA, measured through LFP, is used as the primary measure of sleep. SWA can also be measured from EEG, and this appears the more common way to define sleep states. Can data be included that quantifies the degree to which these are correlated? Is cortical LFP-measured SWA one hundred percent predictive of SWA derived from EEG? Other indicators of sleep include arousal threshold. Do the authors have data showing relationships between their LFP-measure of SWA and such other measures?

8) Related to this, how are changes in LFP-measured SWA in local cortical areas related to EEG-measured SWA during perturbation experiments? This is partially addressed in Figure 7 by measuring SWA with LFP in another cortical area, but it would be interesting to compare this to a global EEG measure.

9) Is there any possibility that manipulation of astrocytes may directly influence LFP, for example through secretion of ions? It seems unlikely, but not impossible.

results.result: Cortical astrocyte Ca2+ event frequency is negatively correlated with slow-wave activity (SWA) across behavioral states, with Ca2+ events highest during locomotory wake, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during sleep. This relationship is partially dependent on IP3R2, as the correlation is decreased in IP3R2 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 provide converging evidence from correlational analysis (C7), quantitative measurements across behavioral states (C8-C9), and genetic validation using IP3R2 KO mice (C10). The data are internally consistent and the use of knockout mice strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. The statistical analyses appear appropriate for the correlational claims made.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ events are preceded by decreases in SWA and followed by increases in SWA, with this modulation being significantly higher during sleep compared to stationary wake and partially dependent on IP3R2. The authors speculate this may reflect a homeostatic process regulating sleep depth.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 present solid event-triggered average data showing temporal relationships between Ca2+ events and SWA. However, C49 is explicitly speculative and the causal direction cannot be determined from correlational data alone. The homeostatic interpretation (C49) requires additional experimental validation beyond the observational data provided.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes increases Ca2+ event frequency and significantly increases SWA during sleep without affecting total sleep duration or wake SWA. This effect is dependent on IP3R2 and is not due to CNO alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 and C52 provide strong experimental evidence with appropriate controls. The use of within-animal saline controls (C15), CNO-only controls without DREADD expression (C52), and IP3R2 KO validation (C18-C19) demonstrate experimental rigor. The dissociation between sleep depth (increased) and duration (unchanged) is well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes increases SWA primarily through enhancement of delta wave amplitude rather than slow oscillations, with delta waves showing significantly greater amplitude increases than slow oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 provide detailed waveform analysis distinguishing delta waves from slow oscillations. The finding that Gi-DREADD affects delta wave amplitude more than slow oscillation amplitude (C22) is supported by quantitative comparisons. The methodology for distinguishing these waveforms using k-means clustering on peak/trough amplitudes appears sound, though the percentile thresholds used may introduce some subjectivity.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ event rate increases before sleep-to-wake transitions and decreases before wake-to-sleep transitions, with these bidirectional changes being abolished in IP3R2 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 demonstrate consistent patterns in Ca2+ dynamics around state transitions with appropriate genetic validation. The bidirectional nature of the changes (C23-C24) and their dependence on IP3R2 (C25) provide strong evidence for astrocytic involvement in sleep/wake transitions. The analysis dividing periods into thirds (C24) is a reasonable approach to capture dynamics across behavioral epochs.

results.result: Gq-DREADD activation produces a biphasic Ca2+ response with initial increase followed by prolonged suppression. During Ca2+ suppression, mice spent more time in sleep with fewer sleep/wake transitions, while the initial Ca2+ increase decreased sleep time. Gq-DREADD manipulation did not affect SWA. Similar biphasic responses were observed ex vivo with neuromodulator cocktails.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31 and C54-C56 document an unexpected but well-characterized biphasic response to Gq-DREADD activation. The authors appropriately acknowledge this was surprising and provide ex vivo validation (C54-C56). The dissociation between Gq effects (sleep duration but not depth) and Gi effects (depth but not duration) is compelling. However, the interpretation is complicated by the unexpected Ca2+ suppression, and the small sample size for the initial period analysis (n=4, C30) is a limitation.

results.result: Local V1 astrocyte Ca2+ events are associated with SWA changes in contralateral frontal cortex, with increased V1-FC coherence following Ca2+ events. Gi-DREADD activation in V1 increases SWA in contralateral FC primarily through slow oscillation amplitude increases rather than delta waves, with viral expression confirmed to be restricted to V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 and C53 demonstrate cortex-wide effects of local astrocyte manipulation. The immunohistochemistry validation (C53) confirms spatial specificity of the manipulation. The differential effects on slow oscillations (remote) versus delta waves (local) is mechanistically interesting and well-supported. The coherence analysis (C33-C34) provides additional evidence for functional connectivity, though the interpretation that slow oscillations 'travelled' from V1 to FC (C37) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: Astrocytic Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling separately control NREM sleep depth and duration respectively, with differential effects on local versus remote cortex, supporting a model where the cortical astrocyte network serves as a hub for regulating distinct NREM sleep features.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C57, C59, and C61 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. The separation of sleep depth (Gi-mediated) from sleep duration (Gq-mediated) is well-supported by the DREADD experiments. The differential local/remote effects are documented. However, C61 is somewhat interpretive - while the data support astrocytic regulation of distinct sleep features, the 'hub' model is a conceptual framework rather than directly tested hypothesis.

results.result: NREM sleep is characterized by slow-wave electrophysiological activity and underlies critical functions including learning and memory, but is heterogeneous in duration, depth, and spatial distribution across cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 represent established background knowledge about NREM sleep supported by appropriate citations. These are definitional and contextual claims that provide the foundation for the study rather than novel findings.

results.result: Background claims establishing that astrocytes tile the cortex, communicate with neurons, exhibit sleep-related changes, regulate SWA under anesthesia, and utilize GPCR-IP3R2 signaling pathways. Additionally, established knowledge about sleep regulation mechanisms including subcortical control of duration, cortical control of SWA intensity, and differential functions of delta waves versus slow oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C48 and C50-C51 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the rationale and context for the current study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ has far-reaching, cortex-wide effects on SWA and slow oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is a summary statement supported by the experimental data showing effects in contralateral frontal cortex (covered in detail by C32-C37). This represents a valid synthesis of the remote cortical effects demonstrated in the study.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ event frequency and SWA are negatively correlated across behavioral states (wake, stationary wake, sleep), with this relationship being partially dependent on IP3R2 signaling.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'no major concerns' and Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'the paper demonstrates correlations between astrocyte calcium signals and sleep signatures such as slow-wave activity (SWA)' without challenging these foundational correlational findings. The data establishing the inverse relationship is accepted as valid.

results.result: Ca2+ events are preceded by decreases in SWA and followed by increases in SWA, with this modulation being stronger during sleep and partially IP3R2-dependent, suggesting a homeostatic role for astrocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'The temporal relationships between astrocyte signals and SWA changes is complex, with SWA decreasing before astrocyte calcium events and increasing after. This is interpreted as astrocytes having a homeostatic effect on SWA. Causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret, in part because the homeostatic effect may involve more than just astrocytes but also neurons or other cell types.' The reviewers request additional data (neuronal imaging) to clarify temporal relationships and causality.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation increases astrocyte Ca2+ events and significantly increases SWA during sleep (but not wake) without affecting sleep duration, with effects being IP3R2-dependent, demonstrating that astrocytic Gi-GPCR signaling controls sleep depth.
results.evaluation: While Reviewer 1 has 'no major concerns,' Reviewer 2 raises critical issues: 'The authors demonstrate sufficiency, astrocytes can change cortical SWA and sleep duration, but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior because of the difficulty in knocking them out.' Reviewer 2 also questions the inverse relationship between baseline Ca2+ and SWA versus the Gi-DREADD effects, asking whether 'astrocytic calcium may be not directly affect sleep duration or depth, but some other signal downstream of the GPCR.' The reviewers request tempering of claims and addressing alternative interpretations.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation increases SWA by specifically enhancing delta wave amplitude (more than slow oscillations) without changing the rate of these oscillations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these specific findings about differential effects on delta waves versus slow oscillations. Reviewer 1 notes the 'depth of the analyses and the rigor of the approach' and Reviewer 2 acknowledges these as part of the 'multitude of new findings' without raising concerns about this particular result.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ event rates change predictably around sleep-wake transitions (increasing before sleep-to-wake, decreasing before wake-to-sleep), with these changes being IP3R2-dependent.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'Astrocytes show activity changes near SWA changes such as at sleep-wake transitions' without challenging these observational findings. The data on transition-related Ca2+ dynamics is accepted as part of the correlational evidence.

results.result: Gq-DREADD activation produces biphasic Ca2+ dynamics (initial increase then suppression), with the suppression period associated with increased sleep time and reduced sleep-wake transitions, but no effect on SWA, demonstrating that astrocytic Gq-GPCR signaling controls sleep duration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises multiple concerns: (1) 'It is unclear what the true effect of the Gq-DREADDs is on astrocyte calcium because activity is only represented by event rate (extracted by AQuA) and not as Ca concentration,' noting that 'saturated calcium could indicate an "unphysiological" state'; (2) 'The conclusion that "Gq-induced Ca2+ is necessary for sleep-wake transitions" seems somewhat overstated' as 'it was not shown that without Gq sleep-wake transitions disappear' and 'the effect demonstrated is partial'; (3) Questions why IP3R2 KO was not tested in Gq experiments. The reviewers request rephrasing and clarification of mechanisms.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ activity in V1 has remote effects on contralateral frontal cortex, with Gi-DREADD activation in V1 increasing SWA in frontal cortex primarily through enhancement of slow oscillations (not delta waves), suggesting cortex-wide propagation of astrocyte effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges this addresses their concern about local versus global effects, noting 'This is partially addressed in Figure 7 by measuring SWA with LFP in another cortical area.' While they suggest comparing to 'a global EEG measure,' they do not challenge the validity of the remote cortical effects demonstrated. The differential effects on slow oscillations versus delta waves in remote cortex is accepted.

results.result: CNO alone (without DREADD expression) does not alter Ca2+ dynamics or sleep features, serving as a control for DREADD experiments.
results.evaluation: This control experiment is not challenged by reviewers. The editors note concerns about CNO efficacy differences between Gi and Gq DREADDs ('Is CNO is equally efficacious at Gi and Gq DREADDs for downstream signaling in astrocytes?'), but the basic control showing CNO alone has no effect is accepted.

results.result: DREADD expression is localized to V1 injection site without expression in distant frontal cortex recording site.
results.evaluation: This anatomical control is not challenged by reviewers and supports the interpretation of remote effects being due to network propagation rather than direct manipulation of distant astrocytes.

results.result: Ex vivo application of wake-promoting neuromodulators produces biphasic Ca2+ response similar to Gq-DREADD effects (initial increase followed by sustained elevation with loss of dynamics and refractoriness to further stimulation).
results.evaluation: While Reviewer 2 questions whether the Gq-DREADD effects represent 'an "unphysiological" state,' they do not challenge the ex vivo data itself. This mechanistic exploration is accepted as supporting evidence for understanding the Gq-DREADD phenotype.

results.result: Astrocytic regulation of SWA is specifically dependent on the Gi-GPCR pathway (not Gq), demonstrating pathway-specific control of sleep features.
results.evaluation: This conclusion is questioned by Reviewer 2 who asks 'Do these results indicate that astrocytic calcium may be not directly affect sleep duration or depth, but some other signal downstream of the GPCR?' The reviewer also notes the need to address whether effects are through natural pathways, as 'the paper demonstrates sufficiency...but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C7-C10. Both evaluations rate these correlational findings and IP3R2 KO validation as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency and appropriate statistics; peer reviewers note 'no major concerns' and accept the correlational evidence as valid.

Perfect agreement on claims C11-C13, C49. Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN due to inability to determine causality from correlational data. OpenEval notes C49 is 'explicitly speculative' requiring additional validation; Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'Causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret' and requests neuronal imaging data.

Disagreement on claims C14-C19, C52. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing experimental rigor with appropriate controls. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether results demonstrate natural regulation ('sufficiency...but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior') and raising concerns about inverse relationship interpretation. Peer review includes additional claims C4, C58 not in OpenEval grouping.

Agreement on claims C20-C22. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes sound methodology with some subjectivity in thresholds; peer reviewers acknowledge these findings as part of rigorous analyses without raising concerns. Peer review does not include C58 in this grouping.

Perfect agreement on claims C23-C25. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes bidirectional changes and IP3R2 validation; Reviewer 2 acknowledges these transition-related dynamics as accepted correlational evidence without challenge.

Disagreement on claims C26-C31, C54-C56. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED despite acknowledging unexpected findings and small sample limitations. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about: (1) whether saturated calcium represents 'unphysiological' state, (2) overstated conclusions about necessity, (3) lack of IP3R2 KO testing in Gq experiments. Peer review includes additional claims C5, C59 not in OpenEval grouping; OpenEval includes C54-C56 which peer review evaluates separately.

Agreement on claims C32-C37, C53. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes compelling cortex-wide effects with some speculation about 'travelled' interpretation; peer reviewers acknowledge this addresses local versus global concerns and accept the differential remote effects. Peer review includes additional claims C6, C60 not in OpenEval grouping; OpenEval includes C53 which peer review evaluates separately.

Both address ex vivo validation claims C54-C56. OpenEval groups these with in vivo Gq-DREADD results (C26-C31) and rates overall as SUPPORTED. Peer review evaluates C54-C56 separately as SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanistic exploration while questioning whether effects represent 'unphysiological' state in their evaluation of the broader Gq results.

Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether 'astrocytic calcium may be not directly affect sleep duration or depth, but some other signal downstream of the GPCR' and whether effects occur through natural pathways.

Peer review evaluates C52 separately as SUPPORTED, accepting the control while editors note questions about CNO efficacy differences between Gi and Gq DREADDs.
